analysis.one_liner: Gradually cuts the two lowest income tax rates from 15% and 28% to 10% and 23%.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in April 1999 and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have lowered the two income tax rates that apply to most taxable income — 15% and 28% — by half a percentage point each year for ten years, ending at 10% and 23%. The first step (14.5% and 27.5%) would have applied to income starting in 1999. The top tax rates (31%, 36%, and 39.6%) would have stayed exactly where they were.
analysis.who_benefits: Every household with taxable income in the two lower brackets pays less on every dollar earned there. Families in the 15% bracket get a cut on all or most of their income. Households earning into the 28% bracket — roughly $25,000 to $100,000+ for singles and up to about $283,000 for couples at the top of it — save the most in dollars, since the bracket covers the widest income range.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers in the two lower brackets

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the 15% and 28% rates with a 14.5% and 27.5% rate effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1998, then phases each down half a point per year until reaching 10% and 23% in 2008.

Because the lower two brackets cover the first (and largest) chunks of nearly everyone's income, a working family's tax bill falls on every dollar earned up to roughly $43,050 for couples and $25,570 for singles before higher rates kick in.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill has no offsetting tax increase or spending cut, so the lost revenue would have shown up as a larger deficit or as pressure to cut federal programs. Higher earners above the 28% bracket get nothing out of it, but the bill also does not ask them to contribute anything to covering the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury, through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offset for the lost revenue: a rate cut of this breadth would have reduced federal receipts substantially, adding to the deficit or forcing later cuts to spending.

The dollar savings are larger for higher earners. The cut is the same five points in both brackets, but the 28% bracket spans far more income (up to about $283,150 for couples), so households near the top of it save far more each year than a family earning $40,000.
The bill does nothing for the very poorest households, who owe little or no income tax to begin with, and leaves the top rates (31%, 36%, 39.6%) untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: As tax cuts go, this one is broad and honest in shape: it lowers the rates that apply to most people's income and does not add new breaks for any industry or wealth type. But it is unfinanced — the revenue comes out of the Treasury with no plan to replace it — and the biggest dollar winners are households well up the income scale. A family earning $30,000 would notice the difference; the fiscal cost would be spread across everyone who relies on federal programs or pays interest on the national debt.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the tax-writing committee in April 1999 and sat there; the committee never took it up, and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative James Greenwood introduced the Tax Rate Reduction Act on April 15, 1999, joined by three Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
That referral is the last action in the record; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue, and the deficit was not enlarged by this cut. Taxpayers in the two lower brackets kept paying the higher rates, receiving none of the relief the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. James C. Greenwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited three Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 15, 1999 and took no further action on it.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or committee vote during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.note: The 28% bracket stretches far beyond middle-class incomes (up to about $283,150 for joint filers), so these households would have saved the most in dollars. The benefit is a lower tax bill, not a subsidy from other taxpayers.
The bill leaves the 31%, 36%, and 39.6% rates untouched, so top earners get no cut — but they also bear none of the bill's cost. Relative to the broad rate reduction, they come out with the least.
The rate cuts are unfinanced, so the revenue loss lands on the government's books — meaning larger deficits or reduced capacity for federal spending. This is the cost side of the tax cut.
